title: ShopMind AI - Agentic Commerce Assistant
short_description: A shopping assistant agent built at the Razorpay hackathon. It looks up real products through tool calls instead of guessing, asks the shopper before touching the cart or payment, and records every step so the store owner can see why it acted.
description:
ShopMind AI is an agentic e-commerce assistant built for the Razorpay hackathon (AI growth and agentic commerce track). Instead of a prompt-only chatbot, it runs a bounded agent loop: the model has no product knowledge of its own and must call tools to search, compare and check stock in a live PostgreSQL catalog.

Key features:
- Agent loop with tool calling (search_products, compare_products, get_stock), capped at 10 tool calls per turn.
- Human-in-the-loop: add_to_cart and initiate_checkout pause and wait for the shopper to confirm.
- Full AI audit trail: every tool input, output and approval is stored in PostgreSQL.
- Razorpay checkout with server-side pricing, row-level stock locking and signed webhooks.
- Merchant dashboard with an AI Decision Trace, revenue and upsell metrics.
- Campaign agent that looks at abandoned carts and drafts recovery nudges.
- Machine-readable /api/agent-catalog endpoint so other AI agents can discover and buy products.
- Gemini key pool with round-robin rotation and automatic failover on 429 quota errors.
role: Hackathon team project - agent loop, tools and backend
problem: Shopping chatbots often make up products, prices or stock, and letting an AI move money without asking is risky. Merchants also cannot see why the AI recommended something.
solution: An agent that can only answer from verified tool results, must ask the shopper before cart or checkout actions, and records every step so the merchant can review the AI's decisions on a dashboard.
architecture: Shopper chat UI, merchant dashboard and external AI agents call a FastAPI backend (Vercel serverless)
/api/chat runs the agent loop: Gemini decides which tool to call, the backend runs it and returns the result
Money-moving tools pause the loop until the shopper confirms through /api/chat/confirm
Conversation state, products, orders and the ai_actions audit log live in PostgreSQL (Supabase)
Checkout creates a Razorpay order with server-side prices, verifies the HMAC signature and locks stock rows with FOR UPDATE

challenges.challenge: The LLM could invent products or prices.
challenges.fix: Gave it no built-in catalog knowledge, so every product fact has to come from a tool call against the database.

challenges.challenge: Free-tier Gemini keys hit 429 quota errors during demos.
challenges.fix: Built a thread-safe key pool with round-robin rotation and cooldowns. History is stored in Postgres, so switching keys loses no context.

challenges.challenge: Two shoppers buying the last item at the same time could oversell stock.
challenges.fix: Stock is decremented inside a transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE row locking.

challenges.challenge: Raw API errors and tracebacks were leaking into the chat.
challenges.fix: Added an error sanitizer that shows friendly messages to users and keeps full tracebacks in server logs.

results: Working agent that searches, compares, adds to cart and checks out through Razorpay test mode
Merchant dashboard showing an AI Decision Trace for every recommendation
Deployed live on Vercel
learnings: Designing tool schemas and a bounded agent loop
Payment verification, webhooks and transactional stock updates
Handling LLM rate limits in production
next_steps: Add evaluation tests for agent tool choices
Support more product categories and personalised recommendations

title: Linkdine AI - LinkedIn Content Generation Platform
short_description: Turns a short note about your project or internship into a LinkedIn post. It first pulls proven writing patterns from a knowledge base (RAG), then checks and scores what the model writes.
description:
Linkdine AI helps students and professionals write better LinkedIn posts. You either describe something you did (a project, an internship, a certification) and it writes the post, or you paste a draft and it explains what is weak and rewrites it.

Under the hood it is a RAG pipeline: before calling the LLM, it retrieves writing patterns (hook styles, structures, keywords, CTAs) from a knowledge base and uses them to guide generation.

Key features:
- Generate a post from a form: what you did, tools used, tone, audience and length.
- Enhance a draft: hook, readability, keyword and structure analysis, suggestions and a rewrite.
- Quality score for every post (hook, keywords, readability, structure).
- Post history with edit, copy and delete.
- Free and Premium plans with daily usage limits.
- Admin panel to upload CSV/JSON datasets into the knowledge base.
- Pluggable providers: mock, OpenAI or Anthropic, with an optional fallback provider.
role: Solo developer - backend, RAG pipeline, frontend
problem: Students know what they built but struggle to write LinkedIn posts that are clear and engaging. Plain LLM prompts give generic posts that all sound the same.
solution: A full-stack app that grounds generation in real writing patterns retrieved from a knowledge base, validates the output, and scores it, with auth, plans and an admin panel around it.
architecture: Next.js frontend calls a FastAPI REST API (/api/v1) with JWT auth
The request is analysed for topic, category and keywords, then embedded
Hybrid retrieval: pgvector similarity re-ranked with keyword overlap and metadata matches, top K kept
Top results become "content intelligence" (common hooks, structure, CTA style) inside a structured prompt
The LLM output is validated (length, spam, repetition, made-up numbers, prompt leakage), retried once if bad, then scored and saved

challenges.challenge: Pure vector search on a small dataset returned noisy matches.
challenges.fix: Added hybrid re-ranking that combines vector score, keyword overlap and metadata with configurable weights.

challenges.challenge: Storing other people's posts raises privacy concerns.
challenges.fix: The ingestion pipeline cleans text, redacts PII, removes duplicates and keeps only embeddings and derived metadata.

challenges.challenge: User input and retrieved text could be used for prompt injection.
challenges.fix: Both are treated as untrusted and kept in separate prompt sections, and the output is checked for prompt leakage.

challenges.challenge: Development and tests should not need paid API keys.
challenges.fix: Put every provider behind an interface, with a mock LLM and local hashing embeddings, so the full app runs offline.

results: 118 automated tests (95 backend with Pytest, 23 frontend with Vitest)
Precision@5 of about 0.87 on the synthetic RAG evaluation set
OpenAI and Anthropic support with automatic fallback
learnings: How retrieval, prompt design and output validation fit together
Testing a full-stack AI app end to end
next_steps: Curate a larger, real and licensed dataset
Add a cross-encoder reranker and better semantic embeddings
Move tokens to httpOnly cookies and add real payments

title: ZonePredict AI - PUBG Safe-Zone Prediction
short_description: Uses 438 real PUBG matches to test whether machine learning can guess where the next safe zone will be. Seven models are compared against a simple baseline, and the results can be explored on a clickable map.
description:
Can machine learning predict where the next safe zone will appear in PUBG: BATTLEGROUNDS? This project answers that with 438 real PC matches from the official PUBG Developer API, 7 ML and deep learning models and an interactive dashboard.

Key features:
- Data pipeline from raw match telemetry to 3,737 validated zone circles and 2,861 leakage-free training rows, split by match.
- 7 models compared: Linear Regression, Random Forest, Extra Trees, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LSTM and GRU.
- Evaluation on 65 unseen matches against a simple baseline.
- Streamlit + Plotly dashboard where users click on the map to mark zones; it detects the zone number from the fixed zone sizes and blocks predictions when a zone is missing.
- 18 unit tests and 12 notebooks from data collection to final comparison.

Result in short:
- The next zone radius is predicted almost exactly (0.05 m error) because PUBG uses a fixed shrink schedule.
- For the zone centre, no model beats the baseline. Every model reaches R2 = 0.99, but so does the baseline, so the project measures real skill against the baseline instead of trusting R2.
role: Solo developer - data collection, ML, dashboard
problem: Players guess where the next safe zone will appear. I wanted to test, with real data, whether ML can actually predict it.
solution: Collected real match telemetry, built a leakage-free dataset, trained and compared 7 models against a baseline, and shipped the results in an interactive dashboard.
architecture: PUBG Developer API: 438 matches downloaded with an API client
Zone extractor reads LogGameStatePeriodic telemetry into 3,737 validated zone circles
Feature engineering builds 2,861 rows, split by match so no match appears in both train and test
Baselines, Linear Regression, Random Forest, Extra Trees, Gradient Boosting and XGBoost, plus LSTM and GRU in TensorFlow/Keras
Evaluation on 65 unseen matches, shown in a Streamlit + Plotly dashboard

challenges.challenge: Rows from the same match in both train and test sets would leak information.
challenges.fix: Split the data by match, not by row.

challenges.challenge: R2 = 0.99 looked like a great result.
challenges.fix: Compared every model with a simple baseline and showed the baseline scores the same, so R2 hid that there was no real skill for zone position.

challenges.challenge: Users could mark zones out of order or skip one in the dashboard.
challenges.fix: The dashboard detects each zone number from the game's fixed zone sizes and blocks predictions when a zone is missing.

results: The next zone's size is predicted almost perfectly (about 0.05 m off), because the game shrinks zones on a fixed schedule
Showed that the next zone centre behaves like a random point inside the allowed area, so no model beats the baseline
Interactive dashboard and 18 unit tests
learnings: Why baselines matter more than a high R2
Comparing classic ML with sequence models (LSTM, GRU)
next_steps: Try map-aware features such as terrain and player density

title: Expense Tracker Web Application
short_description: A Django app for logging income and expenses, setting budgets and goals, and getting AI tips on spending. Made at the BVC Hackathon and hosted on Render.
description:
A full-stack Django personal finance application for tracking income, expenses, budgets and goals, built for the BVC Hackathon. It includes a server-rendered dashboard, secure authentication, REST APIs, export tools and AI-powered financial insights.

Key features:
- Dashboard with monthly income, expenses, balance, recent transactions and charts.
- Expense and income tracking with categories, payment methods, tags, receipts and recurring entries.
- Budgets with progress tracking and alert thresholds.
- Financial goals with progress and milestone notifications.
- Reports with category breakdowns and exports to CSV, JSON and PDF.
- AI insights powered by Google Gemini.
- Email login, Google OAuth, password reset and TOTP two-factor authentication.
- REST API with JWT authentication and Swagger documentation.
problem: Tracking daily spending in notes or spreadsheets is tedious, and it is hard to see where the money goes or whether you are on budget.
solution: A Django app that records income and expenses, tracks budgets and goals, produces reports and gives AI-generated insights, with secure login and a REST API for other clients.
architecture: accounts app: authentication, profile, sessions, 2FA and exports
core app: expenses, income, budgets, goals, reports and notifications
api app: Django REST Framework serializers and views with SimpleJWT
Django templates with Chart.js for the dashboard; django-apscheduler for recurring entries
Deployed on Render with Gunicorn and WhiteNoise; SQLite in development, PostgreSQL in production

challenges.challenge: Each user's financial data must stay private.
challenges.fix: Used session-based access control and scoped every query to the logged-in user.

challenges.challenge: Recurring expenses had to be added automatically.
challenges.fix: Added a scheduled job with django-apscheduler and a process_recurring management command.

challenges.challenge: Summaries needed totals per category and per month.
challenges.fix: Used database aggregation queries instead of summing in Python.

results: Live on Render, with each user's data kept private behind login
REST API documented with Swagger/OpenAPI
Exports to CSV, JSON and PDF
learnings: Structuring a larger Django project into apps

title: Portfolio Website
short_description: A responsive Django portfolio with file-based content, contact inbox, resume uploads, and production deployment.
description:
A personal portfolio website built with Django using the MVT architecture. The project now uses a file-based content layer for portfolio pages, so projects, skills, certifications, achievements, and education can be updated through JSON files without pushing that content into database tables.

Key backend features:
- File-based content loading for portfolio sections.
- Django templates for server-rendered pages.
- Contact form with validation, spam protection, email delivery, and database-backed message storage.
- Resume download endpoint using Django FileResponse.
- Admin panel kept only for contact messages, resume uploads, and Django user management.
- Static asset delivery through WhiteNoise for Vercel deployment.
- Environment-based configuration for secrets, database, email, and production security.

Why it matters:
This project demonstrates a practical hybrid Django architecture: static portfolio content stays version-controlled in external files, while truly dynamic operational data remains in the database.
problem: I needed one place to show my projects, certificates and learning journey that I could update quickly without touching the database or the admin panel every time.
solution: A Django site where portfolio content lives in version-controlled JSON files, while only truly dynamic data (contact messages, resume uploads) uses the database. Pages are server-rendered with Django templates, enhanced with HTMX for live project search and GSAP for animations.
architecture: Request hits Vercel and is routed to Django through api/wsgi.py
URL router sends it to a view in portfolio_app/views.py
The content loader reads JSON files through Django's cache (keyed by file modification time)
The view renders a Django template; HTMX requests get only a partial template
WhiteNoise serves compressed static files; Postgres stores contact messages

challenges.challenge: Editing projects required database migrations and admin work, and content was lost between deployments.
challenges.fix: Moved portfolio content to JSON files with a validated loader and a validate_content management command.

challenges.challenge: Reading and parsing JSON on every request is wasted work.
challenges.fix: Added Django caching with a key that includes the file's modification time, so edits invalidate the cache automatically.

challenges.challenge: Filtering projects reloaded the whole page.
challenges.fix: Used HTMX to swap only the project grid, while still pushing the URL so filters stay shareable and work without JavaScript.

results: Content updates are a single JSON edit and a git push
Project search and filters update instantly without page reloads
Deployed on Vercel with environment-based production settings
learnings: Choosing the right storage for each kind of data (files vs database)
Production Django settings: secrets, HTTPS, static files
next_steps: Add a blog / learning log from Markdown files
Add GitHub Actions CI to run tests on every push

title: Heart Disease Prediction
short_description: A machine learning project for predicting heart disease risk from health-related input features.
description:
A machine learning project that predicts heart disease risk from user-provided health parameters. The project is useful for explaining the complete ML workflow: data preprocessing, feature selection, model training, evaluation, and exposing predictions through a simple application interface.

Backend and ML workflow:
- Clean and prepare tabular health data.
- Train a supervised classification model using Python ML libraries.
- Accept user input, transform it into the model-ready format, and return a prediction.
- Deploy the app so predictions can be tested from a browser.

Interview angle:
The important part is not only the prediction result, but the workflow: understand the dataset, choose features, train a model, evaluate it honestly, and integrate it with an application users can interact with.
role: ML developer - data preparation, model training, deployment
problem: Heart disease risk depends on many health measurements, and it is hard for a non-expert to see how those factors combine. I wanted to learn the full ML workflow on a real medical dataset.
solution: A supervised classification model trained on tabular health data, served through a backend API and connected to a simple web frontend where users enter their parameters and get a risk prediction.
architecture: Clean and explore the health dataset with Pandas
Select features and train classification models with Scikit-learn
Evaluate models and keep the best one
Serve predictions from a backend deployed on Render
Frontend deployed on Vercel sends user input and shows the result

challenges.challenge: User input from the form did not match the format the model was trained on.
challenges.fix: Built a preprocessing step that converts form input into the exact model-ready feature order and types.

challenges.challenge: Accuracy alone can be misleading on medical data.
challenges.fix: Compared models with multiple evaluation metrics instead of relying on a single score.

results: End-to-end ML app usable from the browser
Separate frontend and backend deployments
learnings: The complete ML lifecycle from raw data to deployed model
Why evaluation must be honest for health-related predictions
Connecting a trained model to a web API
next_steps: Show which features influenced each prediction
Add input validation ranges based on medical guidelines

title: House Price Prediction
short_description: A regression-based ML project for estimating property prices from housing features.
description:
A machine learning regression project that estimates house prices from structured housing data. The project highlights data cleaning, feature engineering, training regression models, and interpreting which features influence the predicted price.

Core workflow:
- Load and clean housing data.
- Handle missing values and encode usable features.
- Train and compare regression models.
- Evaluate predictions using regression metrics.
- Present the result in a simple, explainable way.

Interview angle:
This project is a good example for discussing supervised learning, regression metrics, and why model interpretation is important when predictions affect real-world decisions.
problem: House prices depend on many features, and I wanted to understand how regression models estimate a continuous value and which features matter most.
solution: A regression pipeline that cleans housing data, engineers features, compares several regression models, and visualizes which features drive the predicted price.
architecture: Load and explore the housing data
Handle missing values and encode categorical features
Train and compare regression models
Evaluate with regression metrics
Visualize results with Matplotlib

challenges.challenge: Missing values and categorical columns could not be used by the models directly.
challenges.fix: Imputed missing values and encoded categories as part of a repeatable preprocessing step.

challenges.challenge: Picking a model without a fair comparison.
challenges.fix: Evaluated each model on the same held-out data with the same regression metrics.

learnings: Supervised regression and its evaluation metrics
Why interpretability matters when predictions affect real decisions
next_steps: Deploy the model behind a simple web form

title: Food Analyzer AI
short_description: An in-progress AI project for food image analysis and nutrition-focused insights.
description:
An in-progress AI project focused on analyzing food images and connecting image recognition with nutrition-related insights.

Planned workflow:
- Collect and organize food image data.
- Train or fine-tune an image classification model.
- Return likely food labels from uploaded images.
- Connect predictions with nutrition information.
- Build a user interface for uploading images and reviewing results.

Interview angle:
Because this project is still in progress, it is best to present it honestly as a learning project. Explain the planned pipeline, current challenges, and what you would improve next.
problem: People want quick nutrition information about their meals, but logging food manually is slow.
solution: Planned pipeline: classify food from an uploaded image, then look up nutrition information for the predicted food.
architecture: Collect and organize food image data
Train or fine-tune an image classification model
Return the most likely food labels for an uploaded image
Map predictions to nutrition data
Upload interface for users

challenges.challenge: Food images vary a lot in lighting, angle and portion size.
challenges.fix: Still exploring - planning data augmentation and a pretrained model as the base.

learnings: Planning an ML project before writing code

title: Google Opal AI Workflow App
short_description: An AI-powered workflow app built using Google Opal for experimenting with prompt-based automation.
description:
An AI workflow application created using Google Opal to experiment with no-code and low-code AI app building. The project focuses on designing an AI-powered flow where user input is processed through structured prompts and connected steps to generate useful output.

Core features:
- Built using Google Opal's visual AI app-building environment.
- Designed a prompt-based workflow for handling user input and producing AI-generated responses.
- Used connected blocks and steps to organize the flow logically.
- Helps demonstrate understanding of AI workflow design and prompt engineering.
- Useful for quickly prototyping AI-based tools without building a full backend from scratch.

Interview angle:
This project is useful to explain prompt engineering, AI workflow design, rapid prototyping, and how no-code AI tools can be used to test product ideas before building a full custom application.
problem: I wanted to test an AI product idea quickly without building a full backend first.
solution: Built the workflow in Google Opal's visual builder: user input passes through connected, structured prompt steps that produce the final AI-generated output.
architecture: User input block
Structured prompt steps connected in sequence
AI generation step
Output shown to the user

challenges.challenge: AI output was inconsistent between runs.
challenges.fix: Split the task into smaller structured prompt steps with clear instructions for each.

learnings: Designing AI workflows step by step
When no-code tools are the right choice for prototyping
next_steps: Rebuild the strongest idea as a custom app with an API

title: Dental Clinic AI Chatbot
short_description: An AI receptionist chatbot for dental appointment booking using Retell AI and n8n automation.
description:
An AI-powered dental clinic receptionist system designed to handle patient calls and automate appointment-related tasks. The chatbot acts as a virtual receptionist and helps users with booking, rescheduling, cancellation, and general clinic inquiries.

Core features:
- Handles patient conversations using a voice-based AI receptionist.
- Checks appointment availability using Google Calendar.
- Books dental appointments and stores patient details.
- Supports rescheduling and cancellation flows.
- Logs appointment data and call summaries into Google Sheets.
- Handles transfer call and end-call flows through automation.
- Uses short, clear responses suitable for voice assistant latency.

Interview angle:
This project is strong for explaining AI automation, voice agents, webhook-based backend workflows, n8n automation, API integration, Google Calendar scheduling, Google Sheets logging, and real-world business process automation.
role: Automation developer - voice agent and n8n workflows
problem: A dental clinic receptionist spends much of the day answering calls for booking, rescheduling and cancelling appointments.
solution: A voice AI receptionist built with Retell AI that talks to patients, and n8n workflows behind webhooks that check Google Calendar availability, book or change appointments, and log everything to Google Sheets.
architecture: Patient calls the Retell AI voice agent
The agent calls n8n webhooks for actions
n8n checks availability and books events in Google Calendar
Patient details and call summaries are logged to Google Sheets
Transfer-call and end-call flows handle edge cases

challenges.challenge: Long AI responses feel slow on a voice call.
challenges.fix: Designed short, clear responses suited to voice latency.

challenges.challenge: Rescheduling and cancelling need to find the right existing booking.
challenges.fix: Built separate n8n flows for each action that look up the booking before changing it.

results: Handles booking, rescheduling, cancellation and general questions
Every call is logged with a summary
learnings: Integrating Google Calendar and Sheets APIs

title: Sanskrit Character Recognition
short_description: A FastAPI-based ML and CNN project for recognizing Sanskrit characters and word images.
description:
A machine learning and deep learning based recognition system for uploaded Sanskrit character and word images. The project provides a web interface where users can upload images and get predictions from trained models.

Core features:
- Upload Sanskrit character or word images for prediction.
- FastAPI backend exposes prediction and evaluation APIs.
- Frontend is built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
- Supports multiple model approaches including Pixel MLP, CNN embeddings with Linear SVM, and an end-to-end CNN model.
- Returns unclassified output for blank, low-quality, ambiguous, or out-of-dataset inputs.
- Includes model evaluation endpoints for checking model performance.

Interview angle:
This project is useful to explain computer vision basics, image preprocessing, ML vs CNN model comparison, FastAPI model serving, API-based prediction flow, and how trained ML models are integrated into a web application.
role: ML developer - models, API and frontend
problem: Recognizing handwritten Sanskrit characters and words is difficult, and I wanted to compare classic ML against deep learning on the same task.
solution: A FastAPI backend serving three model approaches (Pixel MLP, CNN embeddings with Linear SVM, and an end-to-end CNN), with an HTML/CSS/JS frontend for uploading images and viewing predictions.
architecture: User uploads an image in the browser
FastAPI preprocesses the image
The selected model predicts the character or word
Low-confidence inputs return 'unclassified'
Evaluation endpoints report model performance

challenges.challenge: Blank, blurry or unrelated images still produced confident-looking wrong answers.
challenges.fix: Added an 'unclassified' output for low-quality, ambiguous or out-of-dataset inputs.

challenges.challenge: Fairly comparing very different models.
challenges.fix: Added evaluation endpoints so every model is measured the same way.

results: Three model approaches compared in one app
Deployed on Render

title: Directory Automation File Sorter
short_description: A Python GUI tool that automatically organizes files into folders based on their extensions.
description:
A desktop automation tool built in Python to organize files inside a selected directory based on their file extensions. The project includes a simple GUI so users can select a folder, preview sorting actions, and then perform the actual organization.

Core features:
- Select a directory using a GUI folder picker.
- Automatically sort files into folders based on file extensions.
- Dry run mode to preview changes before moving files.
- Real-time log viewer to show sorting actions.
- Option to save logs into timestamped text files.
- Uses only Python standard library, making it lightweight and easy to run.

Interview angle:
This project is useful to explain Python automation, file handling, GUI development, OS module usage, safe execution using dry-run mode, logging, and how small automation tools can improve daily productivity.
problem: Download folders quickly become cluttered with hundreds of mixed files.
solution: A Tkinter desktop tool that sorts files into folders by extension, with a dry-run preview, a live log, and optional saved log files.
architecture: Pick a folder with a GUI dialog
Scan files and group them by extension
Dry run shows planned moves
Move files with shutil
Write a timestamped log

challenges.challenge: Moving files by mistake is hard to undo.
challenges.fix: Added a dry-run mode that previews every move before anything changes.

learnings: File handling with os and shutil
next_steps: Add an undo for the last run
